questions.question: Which statement best describes heart failure?
choices: A clinical syndrome of structural or functional cardiac abnormality with impaired forward flow and/or elevated filling pressures
Any ankle edema with normal examination
Only an ejection fraction below a fixed value
A medication list containing a diuretic
questions.explanation: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome. Symptoms, signs, structural data, hemodynamics, and trajectory must be interpreted together.

questions.question: Why does preserved ejection fraction not rule out clinically important heart failure?
choices: HFpEF can involve impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures despite preserved systolic ejection
Only HFrEF causes dyspnea
EF measures every aspect of filling pressure
Patients with HFpEF never need follow-up
questions.explanation: HFpEF can cause serious congestion and functional limitation. EF alone does not capture diastolic function, filling pressures, or the patient’s clinical syndrome.

questions.question: Which finding suggests hypoperfusion in a patient with possible decompensated heart failure?
choices: Cool extremities, confusion, low urine output, or hypotension
Stable exercise tolerance and warm extremities
A normal medication list
An isolated chronic cough
questions.explanation: Hypoperfusion may present with cool extremities, altered mentation, oliguria, severe fatigue, narrow pulse pressure, or hypotension. It can coexist with congestion.

questions.question: A patient has orthopnea, edema, crackles, low BP, lightheadedness, and reduced urine output. What is the priority?
choices: Urgent assessment for congested and hypoperfused physiology
Routine medication refill next month
Assume this is isolated venous insufficiency
Advise waiting until symptoms resolve
questions.explanation: Congestion plus possible hypoperfusion is high risk. Hypotension, oliguria, lightheadedness, and respiratory findings can indicate unsafe outpatient status.

questions.question: Which is a common trigger for heart-failure decompensation?
choices: Missed or inaccessible medicines, NSAIDs, arrhythmia, ischemia, infection, or kidney dysfunction
A working home scale
A completed cardiology visit
Stable medication adherence
questions.explanation: Decompensation often has a reversible trigger. Identifying it is as important as recognizing congestion.

questions.question: What is the primary clinical role of diuretics in heart failure?
choices: Relieve volume congestion and symptoms
Replace all disease-modifying treatment
Eliminate the need for kidney and electrolyte monitoring
Diagnose the cause of dyspnea
questions.explanation: Diuretics help reduce congestion. They are part of a broader individualized plan that may include disease-modifying therapies and monitoring.

questions.question: After a heart-failure medication adjustment, why are kidney function and potassium often reviewed?
choices: Therapy, volume status, and kidney disease can affect renal function and electrolytes
Laboratory values never change treatment safety
Only cholesterol matters in HF
Monitoring is unnecessary if the patient feels well
questions.explanation: Medication and volume changes can alter renal perfusion and potassium. Results require context-based interpretation and appropriate follow-up.

questions.question: Which is a key component of a safe heart-failure discharge follow-up?
choices: Medication reconciliation, symptom/weight education, labs, access assessment, and clear cardiology or HF follow-up
Assume discharge prescriptions were obtained
No review until the next annual visit
Avoid asking about support at home
questions.explanation: Transitions are high risk. The FNP verifies what the patient actually has and understands, assigns follow-up, and closes pending-result loops.

questions.question: Why should an FNP maintain a broad differential for dyspnea and edema in a patient with known HF?
choices: COPD, pneumonia, PE, ACS, arrhythmia, renal/liver disease, anemia, and medication effects can mimic or coexist with HF
A known HF diagnosis explains all future symptoms
Edema proves HF is the only cause
Testing is never useful
questions.explanation: Anchoring on HF can miss a new cardiac, pulmonary, infectious, renal, vascular, or hematologic emergency.

questions.question: When should expedited cardiology or heart-failure-team involvement be considered?
choices: New or uncertain HF, repeated decompensation, difficult therapy, advanced CKD, valvular disease, or recurrent hospitalization
Only after every medication has been stopped
Never for HFpEF
Only for a one-time normal examination
questions.explanation: Specialty collaboration is appropriate as complexity, risk, and treatment intolerance rise. Primary care still coordinates comorbidities and barriers.
